issue_context.title: Zip and Tar don't (re)store directory permissions
issue_context.body:
The Zip and Tar creation / extraction have code for dealing with unix file permissions, but they don't store and restore directory permissions.

cc @eerhardt @carlossanlop
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-system-io-compression See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
The Zip and Tar creation / extraction have code for dealing with unix file permissions, but they don't store and restore directory permissions. cc @eerhardt @carlossanlop
Author: tmds
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.IO.Compression`, `untriaged`
Milestone: -

review_comments: Do we really need a loop here? Can't we just check if `Directory.Exists(parentDir)`? If it exists, then all the parents are there. If it doesn't, then they aren't.

This tracks which directories were created as 'missing' parents. We'll go over them again later to set their permissions at the end of the extract to `DefaultDirectoryMode`, unless we encounter their permissions later in the extract.
Isn't changing this from `PaxTarEntry` to `string` requiring the calling code to now inspect the file system more, since it needs to call stat on the `di.FullName` in order to construct the TarEntry?
We need to call `stat` to get the permissions for the `TarEntry`.
If we don't expect `pendingModes` to be `null`, then the argument in line 70 should not be nullable.
Oh I see why this is null. This is also implemented in Windows, and we always return _and_ expect `null` there. Ignore my suggestion then.

Is it OK to cache this for the lifetime of the process?

Technically this could change overtime of the process, right? Someone else could modify the umask in between two calls to the System.Formats.Tar library.

How common should be expect an umask to change? Can it change within the same user session? Is it possible to affect already running processes with an umask change, or would it only affect new processes?

It's a good point to raise though.

And I can understand why tmds did it this way - There are two places where we need to know the umask. But I wonder if instead of having a `Lazy`, we determine the umask on demand:

- When calling a `TarFile.Extract*` method: The umask could be determined once, at the beginning of calling any of these Extract methods. The umask value can then be passed to any `TarFile.ExtractToFile` internal call, when the entry is a directory.

- When the user extracts an individual entry: If the `TarEntry.ExtractToFile` method is _not_ being called from inside a `TarFile.Extract*` method, we can determine the umask too, if the entry is a directory.

Thoughts?

The `umask` applies to the whole process. Any .NET code that changes the `umask` is not thread-safe.

We should not encourage users to change the umask before using these methods.

If there are use-cases for this, it would be preferable for the API to accept a mask argument so it can work in a thread-safe way.

> We should not encourage users to change the umask before using these methods.

I'm not talking about encouraging people to change the umask of a process. I'm talking about what happens if they do.

Currently, changing the `umask` later won't affect the cached value.

If we determine the `umask` each time the API gets called users may rely on that.

I think we should avoid that and let user create new issues if they need this, so it can be provided through the proper API.

Instead of passing a [nullable value type](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types), why not move the `mode` parameter to the last position and set a default value of `UnixFileMode.None`?

Then the lines below, instead of checking `mode.HasValue`, they could check for `mode is not UnixFileMode.None`.

The reason I'm suggesting this is because I suspect that the boolean logical operations below, which are consuming the `mode` directly, are not really operating on the `mode.Value`, so the result might not be the expected one (Please correct me if I'm wrong here).

```cs
        internal static void CreateDirectory(
            string fullPath,
            bool overwriteMetadata,
            SortedDictionary<string, UnixFileMode>? pendingModes,
            UnixFileMode mode = UnixFileMode.None)
```

> Instead of passing a [nullable value type](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types), why not move the mode parameter to the last position and set a default value of UnixFileMode.None?

`null` is used when we need to create a directory but we don't know the mode from the archive (yet).

A non-`null` mode (including `UnixFileMode.None`) means it is the mode that was stored in the archive for `fullPath`.
How do other 'tar' tools handle these cases? This seems like a lot of extra work. Is this how other tar extraction APIs / tools do it?

`tar` has this type of handling for directories.

I took the two archives that are created by the `UnixFileMode` and `UnixFileModes_RestrictiveParentDir` tests and gave them to `tar` command for extracting.

This is the output interleaved with syscalls for mkdir and chmod:

```
dir
mkdirat(AT_FDCWD, "dir", 0740)          = 0
file
missing_parent/dir
mkdirat(AT_FDCWD, "missing_parent/dir", 0704) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
mkdirat(AT_FDCWD, "missing_parent", 0775) = 0
mkdirat(AT_FDCWD, "missing_parent/dir", 0704) = 0
out_of_order_parent/file
mkdirat(AT_FDCWD, "out_of_order_parent", 0775) = 0
out_of_order_parent
mkdirat(AT_FDCWD, "out_of_order_parent", 0701) = -1 EEXIST (File exists)
fchmodat(AT_FDCWD, "out_of_order_parent", 0701) = 0
```

Here you see the permission being applied when we encounter the `out_of_order_parent` later in the archive.

We don't see a restrictive permission being used initially when the `missing_parent` and `out_of_order_parent` are created. It does seem better to do this, since the archive permissions may be less permissive than the default initially.

```
dir
mkdirat(AT_FDCWD, "dir", 0300)          = 0
dir/file
chmod("/proc/self/fd/3", 000)           = 0
```

Here we see the `dir` being created with minimal permissions needed for extracting.
Then later it is set to the correct permission.

Note that in the common case the archives are ordered: parents come before children. In this case `pendingModes` remains empty.
